passage:
I’ve worked beside Bidisha for four years, and I owe Mr. Anand more than I can say, since he backed me when I was new. So when he told the team to keep the faulty-helmet report “internal” until the audit passed, I nodded like the others.
But a batch of those helmets shipped last week. Someone’s head will be under one, and I keep seeing that.
Bidisha said in the corridor, “Don’t be the one who breaks us.” The word traitor sat in my throat. I said nothing.
I still haven’t decided. Tonight I looked up the ethics line, and I’ve asked for a slot on Monday.
— Rashmi

qa.q: How long has Rashmi worked beside Bidisha?
qa.a: Rashmi has worked beside Bidisha for four years.

qa.q: Why did Rashmi nod along when Mr. Anand said to keep the report internal?
qa.a: Rashmi felt loyal to Mr. Anand, who had backed Rashmi when new, and to the team. Rashmi was also afraid of being seen as a traitor.

qa.q: What small step did Rashmi take after the corridor conversation?
qa.a: Rashmi looked up the ethics line and asked for a slot on Monday. That keeps the choice open and moves toward the people who could be hurt.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have been feeling when saying not to break the team?
qa.a: Bidisha may have been afraid of what exposure would do to the team and its jobs, and may have felt loyalty to the team. The passage shows only the warning.

grounding: Shows a professional pulled between loyalty to the team and a superior and knowing something is wrong, with fear of being called a traitor.

passage:
Mentor note, Friday. Deepika stayed after our review and sat with her hands pressed together. She knows a figure in the client report was changed at director level. She said the director gave her first chance, and the team would call her a traitor. “If I speak up, I’m the one who ends up out,” she said.
I told her the worry was real and did not tell her what to do. I asked whether she wanted to see how the company’s ethics line works, and we read the policy together. She took a copy home.
Next Friday I will check in, and she can tell me as much or as little as she wants.
— Vinita

qa.q: What did Deepika know about the client report?
qa.a: Deepika knew a figure in the report had been changed at director level.

qa.q: What was Deepika feeling when she said she would be the one who ended up out?
qa.a: Deepika was afraid of being labelled a traitor and losing her place. Her pressed hands and the mention of the director's early support show real divided loyalty.

qa.q: What did Vinita do that helped without pushing Deepika?
qa.a: Vinita acknowledged the worry, gave no instructions and offered to go through the ethics line policy together. Deepika took a copy home and kept the choice.

qa.q: How might the team see Deepika if she spoke up?
qa.a: Some might see her as a traitor, which is the fear she names. Others might quietly agree, but the passage does not say.

grounding: Shows a professional torn between loyalty to a director and conscience about a changed figure, and a mentor's support.
